was mostly mortar. The key was under a flowerpot, which
the solicitor's letter had described, with evident disapproval,
as "the customary arrangement."
Inside, it smelled of paraffin and old paper. There were
two rooms downstairs and one above. Every wall that did not
hold a window held a shelf, and every shelf held ledgers: tall,
narrow, bound in green cloth, their spines numbered in
white ink. She counted 112 of them before she gave up.
She took down the nearest one. The first page was dated
3 January 1961. Below the date, in a small upright hand, her
great-uncle had written the time, the wind, the state of the
sea, and then a list of every vessel that had passed the light
between dusk and dawn. There were eleven that night. He
had noted the name of each one where he could read it, and
where he could not he had written "unknown, two masts" or
"unknown, coaster, heading north."
The next page was 4 January, and the page after that was
the 5th. She turned to the middle of the book and then to the
end. He had not missed a night.
It was the same in the next volume, and the one after. She
pulled out a ledger from the far end of the highest shelf and
found it only half full. The last entry was dated 9 March of
the present year, eleven days before he died. Wind south-
west, force 5. Sea moderate. Four vessels. The handwriting
had grown larger and less steady, but the columns were as
straignt as ever.
Nora sat down on the bottom stair. She had come intend-
ing to stay two nights, sign whatever needed signing, and put
the place up for sale. She had a job to go back to, a flat with a
leaking tap, and a train booked for Thursday at 2:15 p.m.
